claims.text: High-temperature strength retention in NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV refractory HEAs is governed by edge dislocations.
Local lattice distortions raise the energy barrier for edge-dislocation glide in refractory HEAs.
Resistance to edge-dislocation glide primarily governs the thermoelastic response of refractory HEAs.
Trace oxygen or nitrogen promotes phase segregation during aging of TiVNbTa at 700°C.
Interstitial oxygen and nitrogen initially contribute to solid-solution strengthening in TiVNbTa.
Impurity-promoted phase segregation depletes solute interstitials from the TiVNbTa matrix during aging.
Depletion of strengthening interstitials produces progressive age softening in TiVNbTa.
Impurity-induced phase segregation disrupts edge-dislocation pinning.
Disruption of edge-dislocation pinning increases edge-dislocation mobility.
Increased edge-dislocation mobility causes mechanical softening in the impurity-dosed alloy.
Oxygen-dosed samples aged at 700°C will retain less yield strength than an ultra-high-purity baseline.
Oxygen-dosed samples will exhibit an earlier onset of mechanical softening than the impurity-minimized baseline.
Oxygen dosing will measurably modify high-temperature thermoelastic moduli.
NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV can serve as single-phase BCC refractory-HEA starting states for the proposed comparison.
The proposed mechanism applies around 700°C while the alloy remains single-phase BCC and uncontrolled oxidation is minimal.

contradictions.description: The conditions compare inert and mildly oxidizing environments, whereas the falsification design requires identical environments and the boundary requires oxidation beyond the controlled impurity level to be minimal. Using different atmospheres would confound bulk oxygen addition with ongoing environmental oxidation.
